implementation_notes: Ruby has no cancellation protocol and no deadline type, so the pattern is hand-written: take one absolute deadline with Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) at ingress, carry it explicitly (a request object or keyword argument), and derive each blocking call's own timeout from the remaining time - Net::HTTP open/read/write timeouts, IO#timeout, database statement timeouts, socket connect timeouts. Timeout.timeout is the only language-level interruption and it is a thread-injected exception rather than cooperation: the official documentation states the block may rescue it or use ensure to prevent it, and that the method cannot be relied on to enforce timeouts for untrusted blocks. Use it only around code known to be re-entrant, guard cleanup with Thread.handle_interrupt, and let a Fiber scheduler implementing timeout_after make the same budget cooperative on IO.
idiom_name: monotonic remaining-budget arithmetic + per-operation timeouts (Timeout only as a last resort)
code_sketch:
DEADLINE = Struct.new(:at)   # Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
def remaining(deadline)
  deadline.at - Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
end

left = remaining(req.deadline)
raise DeadlineExceeded if left <= 0
http = Net::HTTP.new(host, port)
http.open_timeout = http.read_timeout = left   # remaining, not a fresh full timeout
http.request(req_http)
pitfalls: Timeout.timeout can fire inside ensure blocks and cleanup, leaving locks held or state half-written; the docs recommend wrapping it inside begin/ensure and Thread.handle_interrupt(Timeout::Error => :never) where cleanup must not be interrupted - with the caveat that a hang in the guarded region then hangs the thread.
The async exception is delivered only at interruptible points, and native extensions or tight C loops may ignore it entirely, so Timeout is not a reliable deadline for arbitrary code.
Process.clock_gettime must use CLOCK_MONOTONIC: Time.now is wall-clock and moves under NTP, corrupting remaining-time arithmetic.
Ruby threads have no cancellation primitive; a worker that outlives the deadline must be told through a flag or queue and check it at loop boundaries, or it keeps consuming resources.
